title: Five Different Digits
statement: A five-digit positive integer has five different digits and does not begin with $0$. Its tens digit and units digit add up to $9$, and its tens digit is $3$ more than its units digit. How many such integers are there?
hints: Look first at the last two digits. Call the tens digit $t$ and the units digit $u$, and write the two conditions as equations in $t$ and $u$.

The equations for the tens digit $t$ and units digit $u$ are simultaneous linear equations, so they fix both digits. The other three digits can then be counted with the rule of product: choose them one position at a time and multiply the numbers of choices.

The tens digit must be $6$ and the units digit must be $3$. Fill the other positions from the left. The leading digit must avoid $0$, $3$ and $6$, which leaves $7$ choices. The next digit may be $0$ and must avoid the three digits already used, which leaves $7$ choices. The hundreds digit must avoid the four digits already used, which leaves $6$ choices.
solution:
Adding $t+u=9$ and $t-u=3$ gives $t=6$, $u=3$.

The first digit is not $0$, $3$ or $6$, so it has $7$ choices. The second digit differs from $3$, $6$ and the first digit, so it has $10-3=7$ choices ($0$ is allowed). The third digit differs from $3$, $6$ and the first two digits, so it has $10-4=6$ choices.

The total is $7\cdot 7\cdot 6=294$.
